# Asaṅkhata Saṁyutta (SN 43)

**ID:** SN 43
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Asaṅkhata Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0304m.mul8.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Asaṅkhatasaṁyutta* (SN 43) is the forty-third collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated toward the end of the *Saḷāyatanavagga* (PTS SN iv 359–373) [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983]. It serves as a comprehensive compendium describing the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)—the third noble truth, identified with *nibbāna* and defined as the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion (*rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo*)—alongside the practical paths that lead to its realization [Bodhi 2003; Yinshun]. The collection is divided into two sections (*vagga*): the first (*paṭhamo vaggo*, SN 43.1–11) details eleven presentations of the path, opening with mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) and various samādhi practices, while the second vagga expands these presentations across forty-five path factors combined with dozens of epithets for the goal (such as *amata*, *santa*, and *saraṇa*), mostly condensed by repetitive abbreviation [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983; Dhivan and Sagaraghosa 2011]. The discourses conclude with the Buddha's admonition to practice meditation (*jhāyatha*) in secluded places and not be negligent [Polak 2011].

 Comparative analysis reveals differences in content; for instance, SN 43.4 lists the threefold concentration of emptiness (*suññata*), the signless (*animitta*), and the desireless or undirected (*appaṇihita*), an enumeration absent in SĀ 890 [Yinshun; Choong 1999].

- [Choong 1999] Choong Mun-keat, The Notion of Emptiness in Early Buddhism (1999) — Comparison of the three samādhis in SN 43.4 with its Chinese counterpart
